pairing: An isolated S1 and an isolated S2 come from two unrelated processes. If the S2 happens to follow the S1 by less than the maximum drift time, the event builder pairs them and reconstructs one scatter at a fake depth. To first order the rate is R_AC = R_isoS1 × R_isoS2 × Δt_drift; both rates rise after large energy deposits, so in practice the product is evaluated in time bins or with pulses sampled from data. Small pulses are the most frequent, so the fake events pile up at low S1 and low S2, exactly where ⁸B CEvNS and few-GeV WIMPs are searched for. Published rates: XENON1T 0.7–1.1 Hz and 2.6 mHz (S2 > 100 PE); XENONnT SR0 WIMP search 1.5 Hz and 80 mHz with Δt = 2.2 ms; XENONnT ⁸B search about 15 Hz and 0.15 Hz before cuts (several hundred accidental pairs per day), 2.3 Hz and 18–26 mHz after the shadow cuts; LZ predicts 2.8 ± 0.6 accidental events in 220 live days (WS2024) and 6.6 ± 0.3 in its 5.7 t·yr low-mass search (WS2025).

categories.name: Real events with lost charge
categories.summary: An energy deposit gives light, but its electrons never reach the gas: charge-insensitive regions, attachment, or light leaking in from outside.

categories.summary: Electrons from an earlier event that reach the gas late: trapped at the surface, held by impurities, or stuck on walls.

sources.name: Events below the cathode
sources.mechanism: Between the cathode and the bottom screening electrode the field points the other way (reverse-field region), so ionisation electrons drift down to the screen and never reach the gas. The scintillation light is still seen, mostly by the bottom array. The result is an S1 with no S2.
sources.chain: energy deposit below the cathode → light detected, charge drifts away from the gas → S1 with no S2
sources.timescale: prompt; random in time (follows the background rate of the detector)
sources.correlated_with: none (random); rate set by radioactivity of the bottom array, cathode and bottom screen
sources.evidence_note: Named as an S1-only source by LZ (reverse-field region), XENON1T (below-cathode region) and PandaX-II; it is a geometric property of every TPC with a bottom screen.

key_numbers.text: XENON1T lone-S1 rate, all origins together: 0.7–1.1 Hz

sources.mitigation: S1 hit-pattern and top-bottom asymmetry cuts (light concentrated on the bottom array), consistency of the S1 pattern with drift time; argon designs without a reverse-field region avoid it.

sources.name: Charge loss near the wall
sources.mechanism: Close to the wall, and especially in the bottom corner near the cathode, drift-field lines end on the reflector instead of the gate. Electrons from an interaction there are lost on the wall, so the event keeps its S1 and loses all of its S2. Wall charge-up changes the size of this volume with time.
sources.chain: energy deposit near the wall → electrons follow field lines onto the wall → S1 with no S2
sources.timescale: prompt; random in time
sources.correlated_with: none (random); concentrated at large radius and low z
sources.evidence_note: XENONnT models the volume with a field-simulation probability map p_CIV(R,Z) and PandaX-II lists total charge loss near the bottom wall as an S1 origin; its share of the isolated-S1 rate is still being measured (XENON S1-only position reconstruction, LIDINE 2026 round table).

key_numbers.text: DarkSide-20k risk rating for this source: High (the only isolated-S1 source rated high)

sources.mitigation: S1 position reconstruction to remove S1s from the wall, fiducial cuts on paired events, field shaping to shrink the volume.

sources.name: Light leaks from outside
sources.mechanism: Energy deposits in the liquid outside the reflector wall (skin, or the volume around the electrodes) produce scintillation but no collected charge. Part of that light enters the TPC through gaps, holes and the partly transparent reflector and is recorded as a small S1.
sources.chain: energy deposit outside the wall → light leaks into the TPC → S1 with no S2
sources.timescale: prompt; random in time
sources.correlated_with: none (random); coincident with a signal in the skin/veto where one is instrumented
sources.evidence_note: Listed by PandaX-II ('possible light leakage from scattering events outside the TPC'), in the LZ source list reproduced in the LIDINE 2026 overview talk, and by the round table for both xenon and argon ('a prominent one' for argon); no published rate.

DS-20k ESR reflector transmits about 2% of visible light

sources.mitigation: Skin/outer-detector veto, light-tight reflector design, S1 hit-pattern cuts.

sources.name: S1 from the gas phase
sources.mechanism: An interaction in the gas, in particular above the anode where the field does not send electrons through the electroluminescence gap, gives scintillation without a normal S2. The pulse is S1-like but has a gas-like time profile and is seen mostly by the top array.
sources.chain: energy deposit in the gas above the anode → scintillation, no electrons through the gap → S1 with no S2
sources.timescale: prompt; random in time
sources.evidence_note: Listed as an isolated-S1 origin by PandaX-II (region above the anode) and in the LZ source list shown in the LIDINE 2026 overview talk; no published rate.

sources.mitigation: S1 pulse-shape and top-bottom asymmetry cuts.

sources.name: PMT dark-count pile-up
sources.mechanism: Thermal dark counts of different photosensors fall by chance within the S1 coincidence window and satisfy the 2- or 3-fold requirement. The fake S1 has no physical position and a random hit pattern. SiPMs have far higher dark rates per area and add optical crosstalk between devices.
sources.chain: uncorrelated dark counts in 2–3 sensors within the coincidence window → small fake S1
sources.timescale: random; coincidence window of order 100 ns
sources.evidence_note: PandaX-II identifies PMT dark noise as the dominant non-physical origin of isolated S1s; LZ and XENONnT name it too, while the LIDINE 2026 round table judged it a small contribution in today's detectors.

key_numbers.text: PandaX-II dark rate per PMT: 1.9, 0.17 and 0.23 kHz in Runs 9, 10 and 11
Hamamatsu VUV4 and FBK VUV-HD3 SiPMs emit 40 ± 9 and 61 ± 11 secondary photons per avalanche at 4 V overvoltage

sources.mitigation: Higher coincidence fold, low-dark-count sensors, hit-pattern and top-bottom asymmetry cuts.

sources.name: PMT light emission, afterpulses
sources.mechanism: Some PMTs emit low-intensity light ('micro light emission') that other PMTs detect, so one tube injects correlated single photons into the array. Ion afterpulses from a degraded vacuum add delayed hits and can themselves be accompanied by light. These photons build small S1-like coincidences.
sources.chain: light emission or afterpulse in one PMT → photons seen by neighbouring or facing PMTs → small fake S1
sources.timescale: continuous (light emission); afterpulses follow a primary hit after the ion transit time (µs scale)
sources.correlated_with: specific PMTs and their high voltage; afterpulses follow large pulses in the same tube
sources.evidence_note: XENON reports that micro light emission in random coincidence with single-electron signals was a significant accidental-coincidence source in XENON1T; first seen in R11410-20 tubes by Akimov et al.

key_numbers.text: XENONnT qualification: 368 R11410-21 PMTs tested in cryogenic xenon, 26 rejected
R11410-20 tubes with dark count rate above 10 kHz emit single photons, at room temperature and down to -60 °C

sources.mitigation: Screen PMTs for light emission and leaks before installation, lower the voltage of or switch off emitting tubes, exclude them from the coincidence.

sources.importance_note: Reported by XENON as a significant accidental-coincidence source in XENON1T; PMTs are now screened for it, and no share is published for current detectors.

sources.name: Cherenkov light in PMT windows
sources.mechanism: Betas and Compton electrons from radioactivity in or near a PMT cross its quartz window above the Cherenkov threshold. The prompt light is detected mainly by that PMT and a few neighbours, with no ionisation in the liquid.
sources.chain: fast electron in a quartz window → Cherenkov photons → S1-like pulse concentrated in one PMT
sources.timescale: prompt (ns)
sources.evidence_note: Named by LZ as a non-xenon process that appears as an S1, and repeated at the LIDINE 2026 round table; no published rate.

key_numbers.text: DarkSide-20k risk rating: Low (pulse shape; Cherenkov plus an ER can look like a nuclear recoil, but then has an S2)

sources.mitigation: Cut on the fraction of S1 light in a single PMT and on pulse shape (Cherenkov is faster than scintillation).

sources.name: Cherenkov light in PTFE
sources.mechanism: Electrons from decays in or near the PTFE reflector produce Cherenkov light inside the PTFE, which is transparent enough for part of it to reach the photosensors. No charge is produced in the active liquid.
sources.chain: fast electron in PTFE → Cherenkov photons → small S1 with no S2
sources.timescale: prompt (ns)
sources.evidence_note: In the LZ source list reproduced in the LIDINE 2026 overview talk and in the round-table minutes (in argon it is removed by cuts and by replacing PTFE with ESR); no published rate.
sources.mitigation: Pulse-shape and hit-pattern cuts; DarkSide-20k removes PTFE from the design.

sources.name: Quartz window fluorescence
sources.mechanism: VUV light from a large S1 or S2 excites the fused-silica windows of the photosensors, which re-emit longer-wavelength photons with a power-law time profile. These delayed single photons pile up into 2–3-fold S1s. The effect does not depend on xenon purity or field.
sources.chain: large S1/S2 → VUV excites quartz windows → delayed single photons (power law) → pile-up into small S1
sources.timescale: µs to ms after a large pulse, power law; whether it still dominates at 5 ms–1 s is open
sources.evidence_note: Sorensen and Gibbons (LBNL) showed it is the dominant delayed-photon component below 5 ms in their cell: the noise survives removal of PTFE, grid, liquid surface and xenon, and drops with a windowless SiPM; XENONnT lone-hit data suggest it is not the only source at later times.

key_numbers.text: Delayed photon noise drops about 20-fold with a windowless SiPM (LBNL cell, t < 5 ms)
LZ: about 48% of 3-fold isolated S1s (0.55 Hz in WS2024) are pile-up of non-VUV single photons

sources.mitigation: Time veto after large pulses (shadow cut), windowless or different-window photosensors, higher S1 coincidence fold.

sources.name: PTFE fluorescence
sources.mechanism: VUV scintillation absorbed in the PTFE reflector would be re-emitted with a delay as visible or near-UV photons, giving single-photon hits that pile up into S1s after large signals. Bench tests disagree on whether PTFE itself does this at a relevant level.
sources.chain: large S1/S2 → VUV absorbed in PTFE → delayed photons → pile-up into small S1
sources.timescale: µs to s after a large pulse (assumed power law)
sources.evidence_note: It is in the LZ source list and was the working hypothesis of the LZ isolated-S1 study, but at LBNL replacing PTFE with aluminium left the delayed photons unchanged, and TUM found no photoluminescence from a LUX PTFE batch at room temperature.

key_numbers.text: PTFE (LUX batch) wavelength-shifting efficiency below 0.05–0.35% of TPB for 130–250 nm excitation, 400–550 nm emission, room temperature
DarkSide-20k risk rating: Low (pulse shape, and PTFE removed from the design)

sources.mitigation: Time veto after large pulses; material choice and screening.

sources.name: Flux residue and particulates
sources.mechanism: Solder-flux residue on PMT bases and cables, and particulates that flake off into the detector, photoluminesce in the visible when hit by VUV light. The emission would add delayed non-VUV photons that are not tied to the position of the photosensor windows.
sources.chain: large S1/S2 → VUV excites flux residue or particulates → delayed visible photons → pile-up into small S1
sources.timescale: not yet measured (no published decay constants)
sources.evidence_note: Nikhef measured photoluminescence of the solder fluxes used in XENONnT and LZ under 120–310 nm light; that it contributes to isolated S1s in a detector is not yet shown.

key_numbers.text: Flux residues photoluminesce at a few per cent of PEN (efficiency of order 1%); for KS115 the yield rises 2.4-fold at liquid-xenon temperature

sources.mitigation: Cleaning and material screening; time veto after large pulses.

sources.importance_note: Photoluminescence of the flux residues is measured on the bench; a contribution to isolated S1s in a detector is not yet shown.

sources.name: Delayed photon trains
sources.mechanism: After every large S2 (and after muons) the rate of single-photon hits stays raised for up to seconds. Chance overlaps of these hits form 2–3-fold S1s. This is the observed population; window fluorescence, material photoluminescence and PMT effects are the candidate origins, listed as separate entries.
sources.chain: large S2 or muon → raised single-photon rate for ms–s → 2–3 hits coincide → small S1
sources.timescale: ms to s after a large S2: power law (LZ index -0.83; XENONnT cut-off near 0.3 s); exponential with 2.3 s after muons (LZ)
sources.correlated_with: preceding large S2 (time; in XENONnT only weakly with its hit pattern), muons, high-energy events
sources.evidence_note: Measured in LUX, LZ (non-VUV photons identified with the double-photoelectron effect) and XENONnT (lone-hit rate after large S2s); XENONnT names delayed signals after high-energy interactions as the primary source of isolated S1s and S2s in its ⁸B search.

key_numbers.text: LZ: about 48% of 3-fold isolated S1s (0.55 Hz in WS2024) are non-VUV single-photon pile-up; rate after large S2s follows a power law with index -0.83
XENONnT: delayed lone-hit rate follows a power law with a cut-off at about 0.28 s
XENONnT ⁸B search: isolated-S1 rate about 15 Hz before cuts
XENONnT ⁸B search: isolated-S1 rate 2.3 (2.2) Hz after all cuts in SR0 (SR1)
LUX: delayed photoelectron rate in the top and bottom arrays in a ratio of about 1:2

sources.mitigation: Time-shadow veto after large pulses (S2_prev/Δt_prev), exclusion of high-rate periods, S1 BDT on shape and hit pattern.

sources.name: Single electrons tagged as S1
sources.mechanism: A single extracted electron gives a small electroluminescence pulse. Near the classification boundary the reconstruction can label it S1 instead of S2. The abundant delayed single electrons then feed the isolated-S1 sample.
sources.chain: single electron extracted → small electroluminescence pulse → classified as S1 by the peak classifier
sources.timescale: follows the single-electron rate: ms–s after large S2s
sources.correlated_with: preceding large S2 (time and xy position)
sources.evidence_note: XENONnT lists misclassified single electrons as a plausible origin of fake S1s in its analysis papers, PandaX-II lists it too, and the round table repeated it; the fraction is not published.
sources.mitigation: Peak-classification cuts on width and area fraction top, S1 BDT, time-shadow veto.

sources.name: Sparks on electrodes
sources.mechanism: Small discharges on a high-voltage electrode emit a flash of light without producing electrons that drift to the gas. The flash is recorded as an S1-like pulse.
sources.chain: micro-discharge on an electrode → light flash, no drifting charge → S1 with no S2
sources.timescale: random; may come in bursts with high-voltage instabilities
sources.evidence_note: Listed by PandaX-II as a possible physical origin ('tiny sparks on the TPC electrode'); no measurement.
sources.mitigation: Stable high voltage, removal of unstable periods, S1 pattern cuts.

sources.importance_note: No measurement; listed by PandaX-II as a possible origin.

sources.name: S2 lost during the drift
sources.mechanism: For a small energy deposit deep in the TPC, the few ionisation electrons can all be captured by electronegative impurities during the drift, or the surviving S2 can fall below the S2 threshold. The S1 is then left without a partner. The captured electrons may reappear later as delayed single electrons.
sources.chain: low-energy deposit at long drift → electrons attach to impurities or S2 below threshold → S1 with no S2
sources.timescale: prompt; random in time
sources.correlated_with: none (random); worse at low electron lifetime and long drift
sources.evidence_note: Follows from finite electron lifetime and S2 thresholds; XENONnT only says generically that an S1 or S2 can be 'not reconstructed due to detector effects', and no source singles this out or gives a rate.
sources.mitigation: High electron lifetime, low S2 threshold.

sources.name: Radon daughters on the wall
sources.mechanism: ²¹⁰Pb and its daughters plated on the PTFE decay at the surface, where part or all of the ionisation charge is lost on the wall. With partial loss this is the 'surface background' (S1 with a reduced S2); with total loss it is an S1-only event.
sources.chain: decay of plated-out radon daughter on the wall → charge lost on PTFE → S1 with reduced or no S2
sources.timescale: prompt; random in time
sources.evidence_note: The surface background with reduced S2 is modelled from data by XENON1T (PTFE-surface events including ²¹⁰Po alphas); the S1-only limit as an accidental source is inferred, not measured separately from the wall charge-insensitive volume.

key_numbers.text: XENON1T fiducial radius of 42.8 cm chosen to reduce the surface background

sources.mitigation: Radial fiducial cut, S1 position reconstruction, radon-free handling of PTFE.

sources.importance_note: The S1-only contribution has not been measured separately from the wall charge-insensitive volume.

sources.name: Alphas in the ESR reflector
sources.mechanism: Radon daughters deposited on or in the ESR reflector foil emit alphas that make the foil scintillate, or that cross into the thin liquid layer behind it. No charge reaches the gas. This is the dominant isolated-S1 source expected in DarkSide-20k.
sources.chain: alpha decay in or on the ESR foil → scintillation of ESR → S1 with no S2
sources.timescale: prompt; random in time

sources.mechanism: TPB does not re-emit all 127 nm light promptly: triplet states give delayed components from tens of nanoseconds to microseconds. The late photons distort the S1 pulse shape and add single photons after large pulses.

sources.timescale: tens of ns to a few µs after any scintillation pulse
sources.evidence_note: Measured by Segreto (2015) and, on the nanosecond scale, by ARIS; its contribution to isolated S1s in a TPC has not been quantified.

sources.name: Dust in the liquid
sources.mechanism: Dust particles carrying alpha emitters float in the liquid when the flow velocity is below their terminal velocity. An alpha loses part of its energy inside the particle, so the event looks like a low-energy S1; its charge yield is not that of a normal recoil.
sources.chain: alpha decay inside a dust particle → degraded-energy scintillation in the liquid → low-energy S1-like event
sources.timescale: prompt; random in time
sources.evidence_note: Raised at the LIDINE 2026 round table as a concern for argon (dust from plastic coatings, hair, getter zirconium); not quantified as an accidental source.
sources.mitigation: Clean assembly, filtration, control of liquid flow.

sources.name: Delayed electrons (impurity release)
sources.mechanism: During the drift of a large charge cloud, a fraction of the electrons attach to electronegative impurities. They are released later, one by one, drift up and are extracted as single electrons at the xy position of the parent event. Single and piled-up few-electron pulses form small S2s. What triggers the release (thermal, field, or photodetachment by delayed photons) is not settled.
sources.chain: large S2 → electrons captured on impurities along the drift path → released ms–s later → single/few-electron S2s
sources.timescale: ms to ~1 s after a large S2, power law close to t^-1 (LZ: index -1.13; LUX: -1.0 to -1.1)
sources.correlated_with: preceding large S2: time, xy position, S2 size and drift time of the parent
sources.evidence_note: LZ shows that the train amplitude scales with the electrons lost to impurities during the drift while the power law is insensitive to fields and purity; XENON1T and LUX reach the same conclusion, and the UCSD single-phase detector sees the train with no liquid surface at all.

key_numbers.text: LZ: delayed single electrons follow a power law with index -1.13 at nominal field
XENON1T: t^-1 power law over O(100) drift times, within a few cm of the parent S2
XENONnT SR0: isolated-S2 rate 80 mHz, an order of magnitude above XENON1T, attributed to more delayed electrons
Single-phase liquid xenon detector (no interface): electron train with exponent about -1.05 to -1.07

sources.mitigation: Time and position veto after large S2s (time shadow, position shadow), better purity, exclusion of high-rate periods.

sources.name: Electrons trapped at surface
sources.mechanism: At extraction fields below saturation not every electron crosses the liquid-gas barrier on first arrival. The rest stay under the surface and are emitted later, singly or in bursts, at the xy position of the parent S2. Argon TPCs report close to 100% extraction and do not see this.
sources.chain: large S2 with incomplete extraction → electrons held under the liquid surface → emitted ms later → single electrons and e-bursts
sources.timescale: up to ~10 ms after the S2 (LUX e-bursts; correlation visible to 50 ms)
sources.correlated_with: preceding large S2: time and xy position; extraction field
sources.evidence_note: Sorensen and Kamdin separated a fast component that shrinks with extraction field, LUX tied its e-bursts to unextracted electrons, and RED-100's electron shutter removed this part; LZ finds it subdominant to impurity release.

key_numbers.text: Electron extraction efficiency saturates only between 7.5 and 10.4 kV/cm (field in the liquid)
LUX e-bursts decay in under 10 ms at the position of the parent S2
RED-100: blocking the charge with a second grid lowers the single-electron rate by a factor ~3

sources.mitigation: Higher extraction field, veto in time and xy after large S2s, hardware electron shutter; argon doping of xenon was discussed at the round table.

sources.name: Photoionisation of impurities
sources.mechanism: VUV photons of an S1 or S2 ionise neutral impurities (or negative ions) in the liquid. The freed electrons drift up and give single-electron S2s within one maximum drift time of the parent pulse, anywhere along the light path.
sources.chain: S1 or S2 light → ionises impurities in the bulk → single electrons within one drift time
sources.timescale: within one maximum drift time after the S1 or S2
sources.correlated_with: preceding S1/S2 (time, within one drift time); impurity concentration
sources.evidence_note: Seen in ZEPLIN, XENON100 and LUX; the UCSD sealed TPC shows the rate falls linearly with impurity concentration, and DarkSide-50 measures the same process in argon at a much lower level.

key_numbers.text: DarkSide-50: photoelectron emission probability per unit length one order of magnitude smaller than in LUX

sources.mitigation: Veto of one maximum drift time after large pulses; better purity.

sources.name: Photoemission from the gate
sources.mechanism: Electroluminescence light of an S2 hits the gate wires just below it and ejects photoelectrons. They are extracted after the short gate-to-surface drift and appear as a small pulse on the tail of the S2 or as separate few-electron S2s.
sources.chain: S2 light → photoelectrons from gate wires → few-electron pulse ~µs after the S2
sources.timescale: about 1–2 µs after the S2 (gate-to-surface drift time)
sources.evidence_note: HeXe resolves a gate-photoemission peak after the S2, PIXeY measures photoionisation of grids, and DarkSide-50 finds its multi-electron spurious signals consistent with photoionisation of the steel extraction grid.

sources.name: Gate electron emission (hot spots)
sources.mechanism: Localised spots on the gate wires emit electrons spontaneously, steadily or in episodes, even at stable voltage. The behaviour does not follow Fowler-Nordheim field emission: rates do not rise monotonically with voltage and the surface fields are too low. Surface condition (oxide layer, defects, dust) controls it. In LZ and LUX the electrons are accompanied by a photon.
sources.chain: defect or contaminated spot on a gate wire → electron emission → single/few-electron S2s at fixed xy ('hot spot')
sources.timescale: random or episodic (seconds to hours), not tied to a previous event
sources.correlated_with: xy position of the emitter; a photon about 2.2 µs before the S2 (gate-to-surface drift)
sources.evidence_note: LZ characterised hot-spot emission with extraction-region-only data and showed it can be tagged by the coincident photon; bench studies at Imperial and SLAC linked emission to wire surface quality and showed passivation reduces it.

key_numbers.text: LZ: photon precedes the S2 by about 2.2 µs, the drift time from gate to liquid surface
Imperial: emission from cathodic wires starts at surface fields as low as ~10 kV/cm, with average rates of 10–200 counts/s and outbreaks up to ~10⁶ counts/s

sources.mitigation: Hot-spot veto in time and xy, photon tag, passivation and cleaning of grids (citric or nitric acid), electropolishing.

sources.correlated_with: cathode voltage; xy position of the emitter

sources.name: Radon daughters on the grids
sources.mechanism: ²¹⁰Pb and other ²²²Rn daughters plate out on the grid wires during production and operation. Their decays deposit energy in the high-field liquid next to the wire: the S1 is suppressed by the strong field, and part of the charge is lost on field lines that end below the wire. The result is an S2 with a missing or too-small S1, with a continuous spectrum up to thousands of electrons.
sources.chain: decay of plated-out ²¹⁰Pb chain on a grid wire → S1 suppressed, charge partly collected → S2 with no usable S1
sources.timescale: prompt; random in time
sources.correlated_with: none (random); drift time at the cathode maximum (cathode) or near zero (gate)
sources.evidence_note: LZ and LUX built a first-principles model of this background that agrees with their data; XENONnT's S2-only search treats cathode events from ²¹⁰Pb as a main background.

key_numbers.text: XENONnT S2-only: a BDT on S2 waveform features rejects about 70% of cathode background at about 80% signal efficiency
LUX: a pulse-shape machine-learning cut against electrode events improves low-mass limits by a factor 2–7

sources.mitigation: S2 width and shape (BDT) to tag gate and cathode events, radon-free grid production and storage.

sources.name: Single-electron pile-up

sources.timescale: follows the single-electron rate; includes a constant component
sources.correlated_with: preceding large S2s for the delayed part; none for the constant part

sources.mitigation: Require no other S2 in the preceding maximum drift time, pattern-based separation of electrons at different xy, higher S2 threshold.

sources.correlated_with: unknown; would sit at the wall radius

sources.mitigation: Radial fiducial cut; fewer plastics in the active region.

sources.name: EUV from argon metastables
sources.mechanism: X-ArT found a long-lived scintillation component in liquid argon and attributes it to extreme-UV emission from metastable atomic states. The proposal is that these energetic photons photoionise impurities and produce spurious electrons long after the event.
sources.chain: ionising event → long-lived metastable argon states → EUV photons → photoionisation of impurities → delayed single electrons
sources.timescale: longer than 10 µs after the event
sources.evidence_note: The long-lived light is measured (X-ArT), but in a scintillation-only cell: no electrons were measured, so the link to spurious electrons is a proposal.

key_numbers.text: Long-lived (>10 µs) component is 11.6 ± 0.2% of the Ar2* light in pure argon

sources.mitigation: Xenon doping changes the light emission; purity.

references.title: Impact of extreme ultraviolet radiation on the scintillation of pure and xenon-doped liquid argon

sources.importance_note: Proposal only: no electrons were measured in the scintillation cell.

sources.name: Electrons delayed in gas
sources.mechanism: In two-phase argon the electroluminescence signal has slow components that the Novosibirsk group attributes to drifting electrons temporarily trapped on metastable negative argon ions in the gas and released microseconds later. These lengthen the S2 tail and can add single-electron-like pulses just after an S2.
sources.chain: electrons crossing the gas gap → temporary trapping on negative ions → released µs later → slow S2 tail / late single electrons
sources.timescale: microseconds after the S2 (components of about 5 µs and 40 µs)
sources.correlated_with: preceding S2 (time); electric field in the gap
sources.evidence_note: The slow components are measured on a bench (Bondar et al.); their role as an isolated-S2 source in a dark-matter TPC is the authors' suggestion.

key_numbers.text: Slow electroluminescence components with time constants of about 5 µs and 40 µs at 3–9 Td

sources.mitigation: S2 pulse-shape modelling; veto window after the S2.

references.title: Observation of unusual slow components in electroluminescence signal of two-phase argon detector

sources.importance_note: Its role as an isolated-S2 source in a dark-matter TPC is the authors' suggestion and is not quantified.

sources.name: ³⁹Ar pile-up
sources.mechanism: Two unrelated ³⁹Ar beta decays in the same drift window could be paired as the S1 of one and the S2 of the other; a hypothesis with no published estimate (underground argon lowers the ³⁹Ar rate by a large factor).
sources.chain: two unrelated ³⁹Ar decays within one drift time → wrong S1–S2 pairing
sources.timescale: random
sources.evidence_note: No published estimate of ³⁹Ar pile-up as an accidental-coincidence component; it is not among the sources listed in the LIDINE 2026 overview talk.
sources.mitigation: Underground argon, pulse-shape discrimination, multiplicity cuts.
sources.importance_note: No published estimate of its share.
